title: iOS 27.2 is out: what changed and whether you should update today
metaDescription: iOS 27.2 has arrived with changes to Messages, Apple TV, CarPlay and Siri. Here is what we know, what only showed up in betas, and how to update safely.
excerpt: Apple skipped 27.1 entirely, so this is the first proper update since iOS 27 launched. Here is what is in it and how to update without drama.
answer: iOS 27.2 is out now. According to 9to5Mac it adds new features to Messages and Apple TV, two CarPlay improvements and a new Apple Music icon. The betas also showed Siri AI reaching more languages, but check Apple's release notes for the final list. If you've backed up your phone, most people should update.

sections.heading: Wait, what happened to iOS 27.1?
sections.body:
If you went looking for iOS 27.1 and couldn't find it, relax. It never reached the public. Apple went straight from 27.0 to 27.2, and Macworld spotted it as soon as the first beta appeared.

MacTrast points to the iPhone Duo as the likely reason. Apple's new foldable shipped with 27.1, and that version probably has Duo references in the code that Apple didn't want out in the open yet.

So 27.2 is the first real update for everyone else since iOS 27 arrived in September, which makes it a bigger deal than the number suggests.

9to5Mac says it landed on Monday. The week before, MacRumors had reported that Apple handed out release candidates, which is normally the last stop before a public release.

sections.heading: What's actually new
sections.body:
9to5Mac says the final release adds new features to Messages and Apple TV, two improvements to CarPlay, and a new Apple Music icon plus a few small changes in the Music app. Apple's own release notes will have the exact wording, so give them a look when you update.

Messages is getting the most chatter. A 9to5Mac headline this week called the new feature an instant favourite, though we haven't confirmed every detail ourselves. It fits with something Macworld said earlier: a reply-suggestions feature was pulled from the iOS 27 launch and might come back in 27.2.

Apple TV is simpler. The betas showed profiles arriving in the iPhone app, which until now only worked on the actual Apple TV box. If a few people in your house share one subscription, you'll probably appreciate that.

The betas also had a couple of quirky extras. One reminds you of your anniversary if you ring your partner and have saved the date in Contacts. Another renames Up Next to New Episodes in Apple Podcasts. We haven't seen either in the final version, so treat them as maybes.

sections.heading: Siri AI and the new languages
sections.body:
Apple has said its new Siri AI would launch in English first, as a beta, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish due in October. According to MacTrast and Redmond Pie, the 27.2 betas already included those languages.

UK readers face a catch. 9to5Mac reported that the new Siri won't come to iPhones in the EU because of the Digital Markets Act. The UK isn't in the EU, so that doesn't automatically apply here, but we haven't been able to confirm whether it's switched on in the UK. After you update, check the Siri section in Settings and see what shows up.

9to5Mac also wrote that the most demanding on-device AI features need an iPhone 17 Pro or an iPhone Air, so an older phone might not get everything even on the latest software.

sections.heading: What about the new Health app?
sections.body:
This one is messy. The first 27.2 beta included a redesigned Health app with AI-powered insights, but MacTrast reported that Apple's own developer notes said the app was being tested and wouldn't be in the public 27.2 release. Another site we read talked about a Health overhaul as though it was arriving with this update.

With the sources disagreeing, our advice is not to update just for Health. If it shows up, great. If it doesn't, you haven't missed anything.

sections.heading: How to update without regretting it
sections.body:
Back up first. An iCloud backup or one on your computer only takes a few minutes, and it's a lifesaver if something goes wrong. Next, plug the phone in and join Wi-Fi, because the download can be big and you don't want the battery dying halfway through. If your storage is nearly full, clear some space too, since the update needs room to unpack.

Then go to Settings, General, Software Update, and follow the prompts. On launch day the download can be slow because everyone is grabbing it at once, so don't panic if it crawls.

If you depend on your phone for work and the idea makes you nervous, waiting a few days is fine. Early adopters usually hit any nasty bugs first, and Apple often follows with a quick fix.

sections.heading: So, should you update?
sections.body:
For most people, yes. Updates like this usually mix security and bug fixes in with the new features, and sitting a version behind rarely helps. The people who might hold off are those with a work phone they can't afford to have misbehave.

We haven't lived with 27.2 for a week yet, so this comes from the reporting and beta notes rather than hands-on use. We'll add our own notes on battery life and Messages once we've used it for a while.

If your update looks different from what we've described, let us know and we'll fix the article.

faq.a: Apple skipped it for the public. Reports say 27.1 was reserved for the iPhone Duo, which shipped with that version, so most iPhones went straight to 27.2.
9to5Mac reports new features in Messages and Apple TV, two CarPlay improvements and a new Apple Music icon. Check Apple's release notes for the full list.

faq.q: Does iOS 27.2 include the redesigned Health app?
faq.a: Probably not. The beta included it, but Apple's developer notes said it was only being tested and would not ship in the public 27.2 release.

faq.q: How do I update to iOS 27.2?
faq.a: Back up your iPhone, connect to Wi-Fi and power, then open Settings, General, Software Update and follow the prompts.

faq.q: Is it safe to update straight away?
faq.a: For most people, yes, especially after a backup. If your phone is essential for work, waiting a few days for any early bug reports is a reasonable choice.
